passages.title: Work experience for veterinary science students
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Work experience for veterinary science students"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear two veterinary science students discussing their farm work experience and modules from their course. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.
[00:55] DIANA: Tim, we need to prepare a brief account of the work experience we completed on a farm.

[01:01] TIM: Yes, I really liked my farm, although organizing the placement was difficult. It was a long way away and I can't drive. I had also hoped to stay for a month, but the farm could only take me for two weeks.
[01:15] DIANA: I was fortunate because the farmer allowed me to live on site, so transport wasn't an issue. The hard part was identifying an appropriate farm and getting in touch with it.
[01:28] TIM: Exactly. Most farms don't appear to have websites. I eventually contacted mine through one of my mother's friends, but making that first connection took some effort.
[01:39] DIANA: It certainly did.
[01:41] TIM: My placement mainly involved livestock, particularly sheep, and I loved working with them. I spent most of one night assisting when a you was trying to give birth.
[01:53] DIANA: Were you doing that by yourself?

[01:55] TIM: No, the farmer stayed with me and explained each step. The delivery was complicated, but we succeeded. Seeing the lamb get upright and begin feeding almost immediately was incredibly satisfying.
[02:10] DIANA: I can imagine.
[02:12] TIM: On another occasion, a lamb had a fractured leg. The vet came to set it and described the procedure to me, which was very helpful.
[02:22] DIANA: There were sheep at my farm as well. As it was in a valley, they kept a lowland breed called suffix. The farm had owned other breeds previously, but not while I was there.
[02:35] TIM: Were the suffix raised for meat?
[02:38] DIANA: Yes, that was their main purpose. They're large, sturdy animals.
[02:44] TIM: My farm was in the hills and had another breed, cheviats.
[02:48] DIANA: I've heard their wool is in high demand.
[02:50] TIM: It is. It's extremely durable, so it's often used for carpets.
[02:56] DIANA: Right.
[02:57] TIM: I was surprised by how many supplements are added to animal feed now. Even the chickens received extra vitamins and electrolytes.

[03:06] DIANA: I noticed that too, and those products can be expensive. My farmer said some cost far more than they're worth. He didn't add them routinely, only when the chickens showed a particular need.
[03:20] TIM: Mine took the same view. Some chicken breeds may require more than others, but he said the low priced and premium products are essentially alike.
[03:32] DIANA: Mmm. Did you work with any other livestock? Yes, dairy cattle. I made an embarrassing error in the milking shed.

[03:41] DIANA: I had correctly noted which cows had received antibiotics, so I knew their milk needed a separate container. However, I accidentally poured some of it into the main tank for human consumption. That contaminated the entire batch, which then had to be discarded. The farmer was understandably annoyed.

[04:03] TIM: I asked my farmer how dependent he was on a vet for animal health. I'd read claims that pressure to raise production was harming livestock, but he rejected that. He did say that farmers could carry out certain tasks currently handled by vets, including minor operations.
[04:22] DIANA: My farmer made the same point, although he still believed professional veterinary expertise was essential.
[04:31] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
[05:17] DIANA: We also have to provide a few short comments on last term's modules. Shall we do that now?
[05:25] TIM: Sure. Let's begin with medical terminology.
[05:29] DIANA: I was worried as soon as I saw it on the timetable, especially so early in the course, and I did find it hard.
[05:36] TIM: I had expected it to be difficult, too. But in fact, it was much easier than I'd imagined. What about diet and nutrition?
[05:45] DIANA: It was all right, I suppose.
[05:48] TIM: Do you remember learning how little pet food is checked for contamination compared with food intended for people? I found that genuinely alarming.

[05:59] DIANA: Yes. The module that interested me most was animal disease. We studied domesticated species in different regions, including camels, water buffalo, and alpacas. Many national economies rely on these animals, yet researchers understand surprisingly little about the illnesses that affect them.

[06:21] TIM: I was equally surprised. I assumed much more would be known about controlling or eliminating those diseases. I also loved the wildlife medication module, especially the work done with birds caught in oil spills. That was completely new to me.
[06:38] DIANA: I enjoyed it, too, and I may choose a related topic for my dissertation.
[06:43] TIM: Right, so that is the end of part three.
[06:50] NARRATOR: You now have one minute.

passages.title: Labyrinths
content: 📌 Labyrinths
Definition
a twisting, spiral-shaped route that leads into the centre.
Labyrinths and mazes

Mazes can be described as a form of [ _____ ]People rely on [ _____ ] to identify a route through a maze.The Scandinavian root of 'maze' refers to a state of [ _____ ].Labyrinths symbolise the course of a human life.In many societies, they have been connected with [ _____ ] and prayer.
Early spiral designs
Carved patterns have been discovered on [ _____ ] in many parts of the world.The Pima people included the symbol in woven baskets.The design appeared on ancient Greek [ _____ ]
Walking labyrinths
The biggest remaining turf labyrinth formerly had a large [ _____ ] in the middle.
Modern uses

Thought to improve mental and physical wellbeing; for example, a person's [ _____ ] rate may slow while walking one.Installed in healthcare and fitness centres, as well as prisons.Popular among hospital patients, visitors and staff.People unable to walk can trace a 'finger labyrinth' made from [ _____ ]Studies report less [ _____ ] among people with Alzheimer's disease.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear part of a lecture about the history, meaning and modern uses of labyrinths. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Labyrinths have been part of human culture for more than 4,000 years, and examples of their symbols have been discovered in places as far apart as Turkey, Ireland, Greece, and India.

[01:06] AUDIO: Their designs vary, but each one consists of a winding spiral route that leads towards a central space. There is a single entrance and only one continuous path, so although the walker meets many twists and turns, getting lost is impossible. Nowadays, people often use the word labyrinth as if it meant maze, but the two are not the same. A maze is a kind of puzzle formed from a complicated network of routes.

[01:42] AUDIO: Mazes became fashionable in European gardens during the 15th and 16th centuries, where tall, dense hedges prevented visitors from seeing across them. To reach the center and find the way out, people normally take several wrong turns before applying logic to recognize the pattern. The term maze probably comes from a Scandinavian word describing a state of confusion, and it is also the origin of the word amazing. A traditional labyrinth serves a rather different purpose.

[02:22] AUDIO: Its spiral has long represented the journey of a human life, and reminded people that their lives have direction and meaning. Because following the path is thought to encourage calm, labyrinths have often been used during meditation and prayer in cultures around the world. The oldest known spiral designs were carved into stone. Examples dating from the late Bronze Age have been identified across Europe and in regions extending from Arizona and India to Africa.

[03:00] AUDIO: The Pima people of North America incorporated the circular design into woven baskets as an image of their cosmology. The ancient Greeks placed the same symbol on coins around 4,000 years ago, while Roman labyrinths made from mosaics appeared in villas, bathhouses, and tombs. Northern Europe also developed physical labyrinths that people could walk through. These circular paths were cut directly into turf or grass.

[03:35] AUDIO: Their original purpose is uncertain, although they may have been connected with fertility rituals thousands of years ago. Eleven turf labyrinths still exist, and the largest survivor, at Saffron Walden in England, once had a substantial tree at its center. Labyrinths have undergone a revival in recent times. Supporters believe that walking along the path encourages mindfulness and healing, bringing emotional as well as physical benefits.

[04:13] AUDIO: For instance, a walk may make a person's breathing slower and restore a sense of balance and perspective. This belief has led to labyrinths being installed in spas, health and fitness centers, and even prisons. A leaflet at Colorado Children's Hospital tells patients that a labyrinth can help people remain calm during a crisis. Visitors often find walking one less stressful than waiting in a corridor, and some doctors use the hospital labyrinth during their breaks.

[04:52] AUDIO: Patients who cannot walk can trace a finger labyrinth made from paper while staying in bed. Although the scientific evidence is not yet extensive, many small studies support the claimed benefits. One reported short-term calm, relaxation, and reduced anxiety among people with Alzheimer's disease. So why do labyrinths appeal to people everywhere?
[05:21] AUDIO: Well, that is the end of part four. You now have one minute to check your...

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: Part 1. You will hear a man who has recently moved to Southo speaking to the coordinator of the village volunteer group. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 7. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 7.
[00:51] JANE: Hello, Jane Fairbank speaking.
[00:54] FRANK: Good morning, I'm Frank Pritchard. I've recently retired and moved to Southo, and I'd like to do some voluntary work. I understand that you coordinate volunteering in the village.
[01:05] JANE: Yes, that's right.
[01:07] FRANK: What kinds of jobs are available?
[01:10] JANE: The village library needs some help. We borrow books from the town library, and local people donate books as well. Someone with a car could help with collecting them.
[01:22] FRANK: I have a car, so that would be fine.

[01:25] JANE: The timing is flexible, and we can arrange it around you. We also keep records of every book that is donated or borrowed, including which ones must go back to the town library. We need another person to keep those records up to date.
[01:44] FRANK: I'm comfortable using a computer. I assume the records are computerised.
[01:50] JANE: Yes, they are.
[01:51] FRANK: Does the library have its own purpose-built building? I haven't seen one while walking around the village.
[01:59] JANE: No, it operates from the west room in the village hall. That's the room on your left when you enter.
[02:06] FRANK: I'll have to take a look inside the hall.
[02:09] JANE: It's a lovely building.
[02:11] FRANK: Is there also a lunch club for older residents? Many villages seem to have one.
[02:16] JANE: Yes, and ours is very popular.
[02:20] FRANK: I could provide transport, if that would help.
[02:22] JANE: It certainly would. Some members travel in from nearby villages, so we are always looking for additional drivers.
[02:31] FRANK: Are there smaller groups at the club for particular hobbies? I'd be interested in helping with one or two, especially anything involving art.
[02:40] JANE: Excellent. I'll check which groups need support and contact you.
[02:46] FRANK: Good. Do you ever arrange help for individual residents?
[02:51] JANE: Yes, but usually as a one-off. For example, Mrs Carol needs someone to take her to hospital next week, and we haven't managed to find a driver yet.
[03:03] FRANK: When is her appointment?
[03:04] JANE: It's on Tuesday, and the trip would take the whole morning.
[03:08] FRANK: I can take her.

[03:10] JANE: That would be wonderful, thank you. We also need help at Mr Selisbury's house next week before he moves, as his health prevents him from doing the work himself. Other volunteers will decorate the kitchen, but it would be very helpful if you could do some weeding in the garden.
[03:29] FRANK: I'd be happy to do that. I suppose the day and time can be arranged?
[03:35] JANE: Yes. Tell us what suits you, and we'll inform Mr Selisbury.
[03:40] FRANK: Great.
[03:43] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions eight to ten. Now listen and answer questions eight to ten.

[04:27] JANE: The volunteer group also runs a social event each month, which is a good opportunity to get to know people. The next one is on the 19th of October. It's a quiz planned by two residents who are very good at coming up with unusual questions, and the village hall is always full.
[04:50] FRANK: That sounds enjoyable. Is there anything I can do?
[04:54] JANE: With so many people attending, we need plenty of refreshments during the break. If you could provide something, we'd really appreciate it.
[05:03] FRANK: I'm sure I can. I'll decide what to make and let you know.

[05:08] JANE: Thanks. On the 18th of November, there will be a dance, again in the village hall. We've hired a band that plays music from the 1930s. They performed here before, and many people asked us to invite them back.
[05:25] FRANK: Dancing isn't really my thing, but I'd still like to help.
[05:29] JANE: We sell tickets beforehand, and we need an extra person at the entrance to check them as guests arrive. Otherwise, a queue can build up when everyone comes at the same time.
[05:43] FRANK: That's fine with me.
[05:44] JANE: We're also planning a large New Year's Eve party. It won't be in the village hall. Instead, we're using the Mount Fort Hotel.
[05:54] FRANK: Sorry, which hotel? Mount Fort.
[05:57] JANE: M-O-U-N-T-F-O-R-T. It's a couple of miles outside Southo. The hotel is supplying dinner, and we've already booked a band. What we still need is a poster.
[06:11] JANE: Would you be able to design one?
[06:13] FRANK: Actually, yes. I worked as a graphic designer before I retired, so that's exactly the sort of thing I can do.
[06:22] JANE: Perfect. I'll send you the details, and perhaps you could let me see a draft.

passages.title: Oniton Hall
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Oniton Hall"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: Part 2. You will hear a guide describing Honorton Hall and the activities available there. First, you have some time to look at questions 11-14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11-14.

[00:53] AUDIO: Good morning and welcome to Honorton Hall, one of the biggest estates in this area. I'm Nick, one of the guides. While everyone is seated, I'll give you a short introduction, and then we'll begin our tour. The estate includes the house, gardens, parkland, and farm, and its history goes back to the 14th century.

[01:20] AUDIO: The original house was replaced near the end of the 17th century. Since then, almost every owner has altered the house, usually by constructing rooms such as the ballroom and conservatory, or taking other rooms down. The farm has changed very little, while the present owner has concentrated on improving the flower beds. In the 17th century, Honorton belonged to the wealthy Sir Edward Downs.

[01:54] AUDIO: After a long political career, he wanted to leave politics behind. He built a new house suitable for his large collection of books, paintings, and sculptures, and it became a place where painters, poets, and other creative people could meet. He stopped seeing his former political associates and welcomed talented guests regardless of their income. Until the 1920s or 1930s, an estate like this employed dozens of servants, and we have tried to bring their daily work to life.

[02:37] AUDIO: Old photographs cannot show very much, so during your visit, you will meet volunteers wearing 19th century servants clothes. They demonstrate household tasks and explain the recipes and tools they use. This new arrangement has replaced the audio guide that visitors used previously. I can see several children in today's group.

[03:05] AUDIO: They can dress in clothes like those worn by children in earlier times, and the fine weather should make the adventure playground popular. The newest attraction is a set of child-sized tractors that children can drive around the grounds. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.

[04:15] AUDIO: We will also visit the estate farm where there is plenty to explore. Most of its buildings were constructed in the 18th century, so the area offers a real sense of farming in the past. The dairy once turned milk from the cows into cheese, but that work no longer happens there. Today you can have lunch or afternoon tea inside, or simply stop for coffee and a piece of homemade cake.

[04:46] AUDIO: The large barn is the imposing stone building at the center of the farm. It contains a collection of old agricultural equipment, once used for plowing, sowing seed, and making gates. The items are displays rather than tools for visitors to operate. Another stone building is the small barn.

[05:11] AUDIO: There, visitors can help groom the donkeys and horses, so their coats stay clean. The animals appear to enjoy the attention, and this is especially popular with children. Horses are no longer kept in the stables. The building is now a shop selling gifts, books, our own jams and pickles, as well as clothing and blankets made from the wool of our sheep.

[05:41] AUDIO: The shed is the farm's only brick building. Just outside it, passengers board a horse-drawn carriage for a peaceful tour through the farm and park. The carriages themselves are more than a century old. Finally, there is the parkland, designed in the 18th century around a lake and mature trees.

[06:05] AUDIO: It is home to breeds of cattle and sheep that are now rarely seen on farms. By keeping them here, we are helping prevent their numbers from declining further. All right, if you'd like to follow me. That is the end of part two.
[06:27] AUDIO: You now have one minute to check your answers to part two.

explanation.step1: Phân tích câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa và dự đoán thông tin theo Linearthinking.
explanation.step2: Trích dẫn bài đọc / Audio: "The original house was replaced near the end of the 17th century. Since then, almost every owner has altered the house, usually by constructing rooms such as the ballroom and conservatory, or taking other rooms down. The farm has changed very little, while the present owner has concentrated on improving the flower beds."
explanation.step3: ❓ Câu hỏi : Over the centuries, most of Oniton Hall's owners altered ✅ Đáp án đúng : B. the house. ▶️ Bắt đầu nghe ở : Đoạn người hướng dẫn nói về những thay đổi của khu estate qua các thời kỳ: “The original house was replaced … Since then, almost every owner has altered the house …” ☺️ Giải thích đáp án : Đọc câu hỏi và xác định từ khóa cần nghe: most of the owners + altered (= hầu hết các chủ sở hữu đã thay đổi thứ gì ). Trong bài nghe, người nói nhắc trước: “The original house was replaced …” rồi nói tiếp “almost every owner has altered the house” . Cụm almost every owner tương đương với most of the owners trong câu hỏi. Thông tin quan trọng nhất là altered the house → hầu hết các chủ sở hữu đã thay đổi ngôi nhà . Vì vậy, đáp án đúng là
explanation.step4: Đáp án chính xác: the house.

questions.prompt: What did Sir Edward Downes want Oniton Hall to provide?

a meeting place for artists and writers
questions.correct: a meeting place for artists and writers

explanation.step2: Trích dẫn bài đọc / Audio: "In the 17th century, Honorton belonged to the wealthy Sir Edward Downs. After a long political career, he wanted to leave politics behind. He built a new house suitable for his large collection of books, paintings, and sculptures, and it became a place where painters, poets, and other creative people could meet. He stopped seeing his former political associates and welcomed talented guests regardless of their income."

Trong audio, người nói nhắc rằng sau sự nghiệp chính trị dài, Sir Edward Downs “wanted to leave politics behind” → ông không muốn nơi này gắn với chính trị . Sau đó có thông tin quan trọng: ngôi nhà “became a place where painters, poets, and other creative people could meet” . Painters, poets, a
explanation.step4: Đáp án chính xác: a meeting place for artists and writers

questions.prompt: How can present-day visitors find out about the work done by servants?
options: by listening to an audio guide
by talking to people in period costume
questions.correct: by talking to people in period costume

explanation.step1: Phân tích câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa và dự đoán thông tin theo Linearthinking.
explanation.step2: Trích dẫn bài đọc / Audio: "Until the 1920s or 1930s, an estate like this employed dozens of servants, and we have tried to bring their daily work to life. Old photographs cannot show very much, so during your visit, you will meet volunteers wearing 19th century servants clothes. Trong bài nghe, người nói giải thích rằng khách tham quan sẽ gặp volunteers wearing 19th century servants clothes . Những người này demonstrate household tasks và explain the recipes and tools they use → tức là họ trực tiếp giải thích và cho thấy công việc của người hầu ngày xưa . Vì vậy, cách khách tham
explanation.step4: Đáp án chính xác: by talking to people in period costume

questions.prompt: Which children's attraction was introduced most recently?

explanation.step1: Phân tích câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa và dự đoán thông tin theo Linearthinking.
explanation.step2: Trích dẫn bài đọc / Audio: "I can see several children in today's group. They can dress in clothes like those worn by children in earlier times, and the fine weather should make the adventure playground popular. The newest attraction is a set of child-sized tractors that children can drive around the grounds."
explanation.step3: ❓ Câu hỏi : Which children's attraction was introduced most recently? ✅ Đáp án đúng : B. child-sized tractors ▶️ Bắt đầu nghe ở : Đoạn người nói bắt đầu nhắc đến các hoạt động dành cho trẻ em : “I can see several children in today’s group.” ☺️ Giải thích đáp án : Đọc câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa cần nghe: introduced most recently (= được giới thiệu/gần đây nhất ). Trong audio, người nói lần lượt nhắc đến các hoạt động cho trẻ em: dressing up in historical clothes , the adventure playground , rồi sau đó nói: “The newest attraction is a set of child-sized tractors …” Cụm “the newest attraction” chính là cách paraphrase trực tiếp của “introduced most recently” . Vì vậy, hoạt động/trò chơi dành cho trẻ em được đưa vào gần đây nhất là child-sized t
explanation.step4: Đáp án chính xác: child-sized tractors

questions.prompt: Match the statement/item with the correct option: "dairy"

explanation.step1: Phân tích câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa và dự đoán thông tin theo Linearthinking.
explanation.step2: Trích dẫn bài đọc / Audio: "The dairy once turned milk from the cows into cheese, but that work no longer happens there. Today you can have lunch or afternoon tea inside, or simply stop for coffee and a piece of homemade cake."
explanation.step3: 📌 Tìm vị trí : dairy ✅ Đáp án đúng : D ▶️ Bắt đầu nghe ở : Ngay sau câu “The dairy once turned milk from the cows into cheese, but that work no longer happens there.” ☺️ Giải thích đáp án : Câu hỏi cần tìm dairy , nên trước hết phải nghe đúng phần người nói nhắc đến địa điểm này: “The dairy…” . Người nói giải thích chức năng cũ của dairy là làm pho mát từ sữa bò , nhưng nhấn mạnh rằng việc đó “no longer happens there” → nghĩa là ở đây không còn hoạt động sản xuất sữa/pho mát nữa. Nghe tiếp ngay sau đó: “Today you can have lunch or afternoon tea inside, or simply stop for coffee and a piece of homemade cake.” Các từ khóa lunch , afternoon tea , coffee , cake đều chỉ hoạt động ăn uống → khớp với D. eating and drinking . 🧐 Lưu ý : ❌ B => Dễ
explanation.step4: Đáp án chính xác: eating and drinking

questions.prompt: Match the statement/item with the correct option: "large barn"

explanation.step1: Phân tích câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa và dự đoán thông tin theo Linearthinking.
explanation.step2: Trích dẫn bài đọc / Audio: "The large barn is the imposing stone building at the center of the farm. It contains a collection of old agricultural equipment, once used for plowing, sowing seed, and making gates. The items are displays rather than tools for visitors to operate."
explanation.step3: 📌 Tìm vị trí : large barn ✅ Đáp án đúng : C ▶️ Bắt đầu nghe ở : Ngay sau câu “The large barn is the imposing stone building at the center of the farm.” ☺️ Giải thích đáp án : Câu hỏi yêu cầu tìm hoạt động/gắn nhãn cho large barn , nên phải bám đúng câu giới thiệu địa điểm này: “The large barn is …” . Nghe ngay câu sau: “It contains a collection of old agricultural equipment” → trong large barn có bộ sưu tập các dụng cụ/nông cụ nông nghiệp cũ . Cụm “a collection of old agricultural equipment” khớp trực tiếp với đáp án seeing old farming equipment . Người nói còn nói thêm: “The items are displays rather than tools for visitors to operate.” → các đồ vật này chỉ để xem trưng bày , không phải để khách sử dụng . Vì vậy đáp án đúng là C . 🧐 Lưu
explanation.step4: Đáp án chính xác: seeing old farming equipment

questions.prompt: Match the statement/item with the correct option: "small barn"

explanation.step1: Phân tích câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa và dự đoán thông tin theo Linearthinking.
explanation.step2: Trích dẫn bài đọc / Audio: "Another stone building is the small barn. There, visitors can help groom the donkeys and horses, so their coats stay clean. The animals appear to enjoy the attention, and this is especially popular with children."
explanation.step3: 📌 Tìm vị trí : small barn ✅ Đáp án đúng : G ▶️ Bắt đầu nghe ở : Ngay khi người nói giới thiệu “Another stone building is the small barn.” ☺️ Giải thích đáp án : Câu hỏi yêu cầu tìm hoạt động ở small barn , vì vậy cần bám đúng câu mở đầu: “the small barn” . Ngay sau đó, audio nói: “visitors can help groom the donkeys and horses” . Từ khóa quan trọng là help và groom : help = tham gia phụ giúp groom = chải chuốt, chăm sóc lông cho động vật Vì vậy, hoạt động ở đây là giúp chăm sóc động vật → khớp với G. helping to look after animals . Câu tiếp theo “their coats stay clean” càng xác nhận đây là hoạt động chăm sóc animals , không phải chỉ đứng nhìn. 🧐 Lưu ý : ❌ C => Dễ nhầm nếu nhớ có chỗ trưng bày đồ nông nghiệp, nhưng đó là large barn , khôn
explanation.step4: Đáp án chính xác: helping to look after animals

questions.prompt: Match the statement/item with the correct option: "stables"

explanation.step1: Phân tích câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa và dự đoán thông tin theo Linearthinking.
explanation.step2: Trích dẫn bài đọc / Audio: "Horses are no longer kept in the stables. The building is now a shop selling gifts, books, our own jams and pickles, as well as clothing and blankets made from the wool of our sheep."
explanation.step3: 📌 Tìm vị trí : stables ✅ Đáp án đúng : A ▶️ Bắt đầu nghe ở : Ngay sau câu “Horses are no longer kept in the stables.” ☺️ Giải thích đáp án : Câu hỏi yêu cầu xác định hoạt động ở stables , nên cần nghe đúng câu có nhắc trực tiếp đến stables . Audio nói: “Horses are no longer kept in the stables.” → nghĩa là nơi này không còn dùng để nuôi ngựa nữa. Ngay sau đó, người nói giải thích công dụng hiện tại của tòa nhà: “The building is now a shop…” Từ khóa shop selling gifts, books, jams, pickles, clothing, blankets cho thấy đây là nơi để mua sắm → khớp với shopping . Vì vậy, đáp án đúng là A . 🧐 Lưu ý : ❌ G => Dễ nhầm vì câu trước đó có đoạn “help groom the donkeys and horses” , nhưng hoạt động này diễn ra ở small barn , không phải stables . ❌ C
explanation.step4: Đáp án chính xác: shopping

questions.prompt: Match the statement/item with the correct option: "shed"

explanation.step1: Phân tích câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa và dự đoán thông tin theo Linearthinking.
explanation.step2: Trích dẫn bài đọc / Audio: "The shed is the farm's only brick building. Just outside it, passengers board a horse-drawn carriage for a peaceful tour through the farm and park. The carriages themselves are more than a century old."
explanation.step3: 📌 Tìm vị trí : shed ✅ Đáp án đúng : E ▶️ Bắt đầu nghe ở : Ngay khi người nói giới thiệu “The shed is the farm's only brick building.” ☺️ Giải thích đáp án : Câu hỏi yêu cầu xác định hoạt động gắn với shed , nên cần bám đúng câu mở đầu: “The shed is the farm’s only brick building.” Nghe ngay sau đó, người nói tiếp tục: “Just outside it, passengers board a horse-drawn carriage...” → board nghĩa là lên xe / bắt đầu hành trình . Cụm “for a peaceful tour through the farm and park” cho thấy đây là nơi du khách khởi hành một chuyến đi quanh khu trang trại và công viên. Vì vậy, hoạt động đúng ở shed là starting a trip → E . 🧐 Lưu ý : ❌ D => Dễ nhầm nếu nhớ thông tin về lunch, afternoon tea, coffee and cake , nhưng đó là ở dairy , không phải shed
explanation.step4: Đáp án chính xác: starting a trip

questions.prompt: Match the statement/item with the correct option: "parkland"

explanation.step1: Phân tích câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa và dự đoán thông tin theo Linearthinking.
explanation.step2: Trích dẫn bài đọc / Audio: "Finally, there is the parkland, designed in the 18th century around a lake and mature trees. It is home to breeds of cattle and sheep that are now rarely seen on farms. By keeping them here, we are helping prevent their numbers from declining further."
explanation.step3: 📌 Tìm vị trí : parkland ✅ Đáp án đúng : F ▶️ Bắt đầu nghe ở : Ngay sau câu “Finally, there is the parkland...” ☺️ Giải thích đáp án : Từ khóa cần nghe là parkland , nên khi người nói bắt đầu giới thiệu: “Finally, there is the parkland...” thì đây chính là đoạn chứa đáp án. Nghe tiếp câu sau: “It is home to breeds of cattle and sheep that are now rarely seen on farms.” Cụm “rarely seen” tương ứng với ý hiếm / rare breeds , còn cattle and sheep là animals . Vì vậy, hoạt động/giá trị gắn với parkland là seeing rare breeds of animals → chọn F . 🧐 Lưu ý : ❌ G => Dễ nhầm vì cũng liên quan đến animals , nhưng đoạn nghe không nói khách giúp chăm sóc chúng; chỉ nói đây là nơi có các giống vật nuôi hiếm . ❌ B => Sai vì không có thông tin về milking
explanation.step4: Đáp án chính xác: seeing rare breeds of animals

content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Romeo and Juliet"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: Part 3. You will hear two students, Ed and Gemma, discussing theatre productions of Romeo and Juliet, for an assignment. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 and 22. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 and 22.
[00:56] ED: Did you manage to take notes while we were watching those performances of Romeo and Juliet Gemma?
[01:02] GEMMA: I did, although it wasn't easy. I kept becoming absorbed in the play.

[01:08] ED: The same happened to me, so I stopped writing and recorded my impressions once I got home. Could I compare a few points with you, in case I've left something out? I also want to clarify what the assignment requires.
[01:23] GEMMA: Of course. Talking it over will help, because I may have missed things as well.
[01:30] ED: Great. To begin with, I'm uncertain how much material our reviews ought to contain.
[01:38] GEMMA: Well, I don't think we need to retell the story, particularly since Romeo and Juliet is so widely known.
[01:45] ED: Exactly. If this were an essay, we'd analyze the verse and Shakespeare's imagery, but that isn't the purpose of a review. We need to judge how successful this particular staging was.
[02:00] GEMMA: Yes, we should explain what made the production work, or why it didn't.
[02:06] ED: That includes describing our own emotional response to the performance. We definitely need that.
[02:13] GEMMA: Agreed. And we ought to refer to the director's treatment of specific moments, such as Romeo reaching Juliet's balcony.
[02:23] ED: Or the duel involving Mercutio and Tybalt.
[02:26] GEMMA: Right. It could be useful to discuss the theater itself and the way the space was used, but with only eight hundred words, there probably isn't room.
[02:37] ED: No, there won't be. Okay, that seems clear enough.
[02:43] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-three to thirty. Now listen and answer questions twenty-three to thirty.
[03:27] ED: Shall we move on to the Emporium Theatre's version?
[03:31] GEMMA: Yes. Several elements were very effective, though others caused problems.
[03:37] ED: Let's start with the set.
[03:39] GEMMA: Visually it was remarkable. For me it was probably the outstanding feature of the whole production.
[03:46] ED: I agree that the design was impressive, even if I've come across comparable ideas in other stageings.
[03:54] GEMMA: How did you feel about the lighting? A few scenes were so dark that I struggled to see.
[04:01] ED: It didn't bother me. In the quieter passages it helped establish a different, more suitable mood.
[04:07] GEMMA: Yes, I can see that.
[04:17] ED: And the I'd been expecting a more traditional treatment.
[04:22] GEMMA: So had I. The opening music was excellent, and the musicians were very good. But later, especially in acts two and three, the music hardly contributed, so their talent felt underused.
[04:36] ED: I agree. That was disappointing.
[04:39] GEMMA: The actors' handling of the lines was another weakness. For me they spoke too quickly.
[04:46] ED: I agree there was a problem, but I put it down to insufficient volume, particularly at crucial moments.
[04:53] GEMMA: Really? Their volume wasn't an issue for me.
[04:58] ED: Seeing several different versions has been quite revealing, hasn't it?
[05:03] GEMMA: Absolutely. It's shown me how contemporary the play can still feel.
[05:09] ED: Yes, society has changed enormously since Shakespeare's day, but conflict between teenagers and their parents is still familiar.
[05:19] GEMMA: Exactly. Young audiences can recognize that family tension more readily than the extreme violence and passion.
[05:28] ED: What was it like seeing the play performed in translation?
[05:33] GEMMA: Fascinating. I'd expected it to be hard to follow, yet I understood the action without much trouble.
[05:40] ED: Once I stopped worrying about every unfamiliar word, I concentrated on the actors' faces. The ending had a strong effect on me.
[05:49] GEMMA: Me too. In fact, that made the emotion feel even more intense.
[05:56] ED: Apparently Shakespeare has been translated into more languages than any other author.
[06:02] GEMMA: Why do you think his work appeals so widely?
[06:06] ED: I read that the plays deal with fundamental themes understood by people everywhere.

[06:11] GEMMA: Yes, and they can be read at several different levels. The characters are also remarkably complex, which means directors can keep exploring them and offer fresh interpretations. Exactly. And that's essential because...
[06:32] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three. You now have one minute to check your answers to part three.

content: 📌 The impact of digital technology on the Icelandic language
The Icelandic language
around [ _____ ] people speak itits [ _____ ] continues to expandit has altered very little over roughly a thousand yearsit has separate terms for digital ideas, including web browser and [ _____ ]
Young speakers

make extensive use of devices such as [ _____ ]are rapidly becoming [ _____ ]sometimes hold conversations entirely in English in the school [ _____ ]can describe what appears in a [ _____ ] more easily in English than in Icelandic
Technology and internet companies

The Icelandic government

has created a fund to increase the amount of Icelandic digital materialexpects the language to remain securefears that young people could lose their Icelandic [ _____ ]is concerned that children may not become [ _____ ] in either Icelandic or English
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear part of a lecture about the influence of digital technology on the Icelandic language. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. All right, everyone, let's begin.

[00:57] AUDIO: In recent classes, we have examined why certain languages around the world are weakening. Today, I want to consider another influence on languages and their users—technology, particularly its digital forms. To show what this can mean, I will use Icelandic as our case study. It is spoken by about 321,000 people, the majority living on Iceland, the North Atlantic island.

[01:26] AUDIO: Its main difficulty is not simply its relatively small number of users, nor is Icelandic steadily surrendering words to English. In fact, its vocabulary keeps expanding. When a new idea needs a name, Icelandic speakers usually coin a term instead of importing one. This is unusual because the language has changed remarkably little over the last millennium, yet it can still express modern technological concepts.

[02:00] AUDIO: The Icelandic term for a web browser, for instance, comes from their verb meaning to wander, which seems very appropriate for moving around online. They also have their own word for a podcast, although I won't attempt to pronounce it. So Icelandic remains active and adaptable. The concern is that younger Icelanders spend so much time in an online environment dominated by English.

[02:28] AUDIO: Smartphones are an obvious example. Although they are a recent invention, young people now use them constantly for reading, films, games, music, and much more. This exposure has advantages since they are becoming bilingual at remarkable speed. But the scale and pace of English influence in digital life are extraordinary.

[02:53] AUDIO: Their parents and grandparents are less vulnerable because their Icelandic is already fully established. The effect on younger speakers is more worrying. Teachers report that teenagers may conduct entire conversations in English in the school playground. With younger pupils, some find it easier to identify the contents of a picture in English than in Icelandic.

[03:19] AUDIO: This creates a genuine possibility that the next generation could lose command of its first language. Icelandic is not the only European language facing this pressure. A technology company may be prepared to support French, but it is difficult to justify the same investment for a language whose entire population is comparable with that of a single French town, such as Nice. A further obstacle is Icelandic grammar, which is far more complicated than that of most languages.

[03:54] AUDIO: At present, the major internet firms show little interest in dealing with it. What response has the Icelandic government made? It is putting substantial funding into language technology, aiming to generate Icelandic apps, social media services, and other online systems. Even with that support, the task will be difficult.

[04:19] AUDIO: There are reasons for confidence. Icelandic remains the official language of both education and government, has survived for more than a millennium, and specialists believe its long-term future within Iceland is secure. Nevertheless, among younger people, it is increasingly becoming their second choice. That situation prompts serious questions.

[04:44] AUDIO: Since a language carries so much of a community's past, could young Icelanders eventually lose their sense of identity? The government is also concerned about children acquiring two languages by separate routes without becoming fully fluent in either one. If that happens, will they be able to express their ideas adequately? That is the end of part four.
[05:14] AUDIO: You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.

passages.title: Advice on surfing holidays
content: 📌 Advice on surfing holidays
Jack's advice
Says surfing is suitable for [ _____ ] holidays during summer.Travellers should be reasonably [ _____ ].
Irish surfing locations
County Clare
Lahinch offers some high-standard [ _____ ] as well as surf schools.Well-known cliffs can be visited nearby.
County Mayo
A recommended surf school is at [ _____ ] beach.The children's surf camp runs for one [ _____ ].Visitors can also see the local [ _____ ] from a kayak.
Weather
Preferred month for a trip: [ _____ ].Typical summer temperature: about [ _____ ] degrees.
Costs
Equipment
Daily hire of a wetsuit and surfboard: [ _____ ] euros.Hiring [ _____ ] is recommended to keep feet warm.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: Part one. You will hear a woman asking her friend Jack for advice about taking a surfing holiday in Ireland. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.
[00:54] WOMAN: Jack, I'm considering taking the children to the coast for a surfing holiday this summer, and I thought I'd get your advice since you know so much about it.

[01:03] JACK: I wouldn't call myself an expert, but I have served quite a lot over the years. I'd certainly recommend it. It works particularly well as a family holiday because people of almost any age or ability can take part. My youngest was only three when he began.
[01:24] WOMAN: Really? It must take a fair amount of physical effort, though. I've been told you have to be reasonably fit.
[01:34] JACK: That's true. If you are, you'll pick it up faster, and you won't become tired so quickly.
[01:43] WOMAN: We should manage that. You've gone surfing in Ireland several times, haven't you?
[01:49] JACK: Yes, and the conditions can be excellent, although a lot of people don't realise that.
[01:57] WOMAN: Which places would you suggest? There seem to be plenty to choose from.
[02:02] JACK: There are. We were in County Donegal last year, and it has several very good surfing spots.
[02:11] WOMAN: I've also read that County Clare is a strong choice for surfing.
[02:15] JACK: Definitely. I've visited more than once. La Hinch is where most visitors go. My children really enjoy it, the waves are manageable, and the town has a lot going on.
[02:30] WOMAN: Is the accommodation there any good?
[02:32] JACK: Yes, there are some high-quality hotels, as well as simpler hostels and campsites, and if you want tuition, the surf schools are very good.
[02:46] WOMAN: That sounds promising.
[02:48] JACK: There's plenty to visit nearby, too, including those famous cliffs. I can't remember what they're called now.
[02:56] WOMAN: Never mind. I'll be able to find the name.

[03:00] JACK: County Mayo is another place I've surfed. It isn't as widely known for the sport, but we had an excellent trip there when the children were smaller. There's a good school at Caroneski Beach.
[03:14] WOMAN: Could you spell that for me?
[03:16] JACK: C-A-R-R-O-W-N-I-S-K-E-Y Got it. During the summer, they run a surf camp for children aged 10 to 16, and I enrolled mine in it.
[03:33] WOMAN: How long did the camp run?
[03:35] JACK: They had three hours of instruction each day for a week. It was ideal, and they were completely worn out afterwards.
[03:45] WOMAN: I'm not surprised.
[03:47] JACK: While they were at the camp, we hired kayaks and explored the bay close by. It's a really attractive area.
[03:57] WOMAN: I'd enjoy that.
[04:02] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 7 to 10.
[04:47] WOMAN: The only time I've been to Ireland, it seemed to rain nearly every day.
[04:53] JACK: Yes, the rain can be an issue, though it doesn't actually stop you from surfing.
[05:00] WOMAN: Somehow it doesn't sound quite as enjoyable.
[05:03] JACK: The weather was good on my last couple of visits. In fact, August is generally wetter than spring or autumn. I prefer September because by then the sea is warmer.
[05:18] WOMAN: Unfortunately, the children will have returned to school then.
[05:21] JACK: I know. Still, an advantage of summer in Ireland is that it rarely becomes too hot. The average is roughly 19 degrees, and it normally stays below 25.
[05:37] WOMAN: That seems comfortable. What should I budget for?

[05:41] JACK: It's quite an inexpensive holiday, since hiring the gear is really the only expense. A wetsuit and board cost around 30 euros a day. If you rent them for a whole week, though, you can save about 40 euros.
[05:59] WOMAN: That's fairly reasonable.
[06:01] JACK: Yes. Just check that the wetsuits are good quality. Otherwise, you'll all feel too cold. I'd also hire boots.
[06:11] JACK: They keep your feet warm and make surfing easier as well.
[06:16] WOMAN: Right. Thanks very much for all your help.
[06:20] NARRATOR: That is the end of part one. You now have one minute to check your answers to part one.

passages.title: Childcare Service
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Childcare Service"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: Part 2. You will hear the manager of a school's extended hours childcare service giving information to parents. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

[00:53] AUDIO: Good afternoon. I'm Mrs Carter and I'm responsible for the childcare we provide before and after the school day. I hope you've been able to look around and speak to some of our staff and pupils. Many of you may be considering the service for when your child starts here.

[01:14] AUDIO: Some parents already know how it works, but I'll explain the main points for anyone who doesn't. We look after children aged 4 to 11, both before lessons begin and once school has finished. Working parents in particular tell us how valuable this is and you can be confident that your child will receive excellent care. Our insurance allows us to have a maximum of 70 children at any session, though attendance is hardly ever that high.

[01:49] AUDIO: Afternoons normally attract about 50 to 60 children, while the breakfast session has roughly half as many. There are currently 70 names on our register, but they don't all come every day. The extended hours service has actually been operating for 10 years and it has developed considerably since the early days when only around 20 children attended regularly. We do our best to keep the fees affordable and believe the service represents good value.

[02:23] AUDIO: A full afternoon from 3.30 until 6pm costs £7.20. Alternatively, one hour is £3.50 and staying for two hours costs £5.70. Meals and snacks are covered by the fee. We provide breakfast in the morning, followed by a healthy snack as soon as school ends. At 5pm, the children receive a more substantial dish, perhaps pasta or a casserole. Please tell us about any food allergies so that we can offer an appropriate alternative.

[03:08] AUDIO: The service continues during school holidays, opening from 8am until 6pm. We arrange a varied programme so that it doesn't feel like another school day. Holiday sessions also give children the opportunity to meet pupils from other schools. We can offer them places because many of our regular term-time children don't attend every day during the holidays.

[03:37] AUDIO: Parents have sometimes asked whether children older than 11 may accompany younger siblings, but our insurance means that isn't possible. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20. I'll now describe several activities available in the after-school sessions.

[04:40] AUDIO: Children can always use the playground, computers and library. And on most days, we also provide at least one special activity. Spanish is one example. Every Thursday, a specialist teacher introduces the language through songs and games.

[05:01] AUDIO: There are separate sessions for younger children and those over eight. Spanish is the only activity for which we ask families to pay an additional charge, although we think it offers excellent value. Music takes place once a week. We're fortunate that a member of staff plays in a folk band, and on Mondays she leads singing and percussion groups.

[05:27] AUDIO: These sessions depend on support from parents, so we'd be very pleased to hear from anyone who sings or plays an instrument and could assist. Painting remains one of the children's favourite choices. Initially, we were reluctant to offer it because it creates so much mess. However, the children repeatedly asked for an art activity, so in the end we agreed.

[05:54] AUDIO: It also gives them a good way to unwind after a full day of lessons. We've wanted to provide yoga for quite a while, but until recently we couldn't find a suitable instructor. We now have someone available, so this is a new addition. We'll see how it develops, and we hope the children gain a range of benefits from it.

[06:18] AUDIO: Cooking is popular too, with the children making a different cake, pizza or loaf each week. The younger ones enjoy it, but they left too much clearing up. For that reason, participation is now limited to children over eight, who can manage the cleaning more independently. That is the end of part two.
[06:46] AUDIO: You now have one minute to check your answers to part two.

passages.title: Holly's Work Placement Tutorial
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Holly's Work Placement Tutorial"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: Part 3. You will hear Holly discussing her work placement with her tutor. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
[00:54] HOLLY: Good morning, Dr. Green. I've come to discuss my work placement with you.
[00:59] TUTOR: Ah, yes. You must be Holly.
[01:03] HOLLY: That's right.
[01:03] TUTOR: So, tell me, which placement have you selected?
[01:08] HOLLY: I've chosen the one at Orion Stadium. I'll be helping to organise a sports competition there for children from primary schools.
[01:18] TUTOR: Yes, that placement is always popular, although dealing with young children can be more demanding than people expect.
[01:26] HOLLY: I realise that. What really appealed to me was the chance to work in the open air. An indoor event might be enjoyable, but it wouldn't attract me in the same way.
[01:40] TUTOR: Fair enough. Of course, safety will be a major issue when you plan the event.
[01:46] HOLLY: Yes, I've been considering that already. I thought I'd have to inspect all the sports equipment for damage.
[01:52] TUTOR: The schools will actually be responsible for their own equipment. You'll be accountable for the site and everything happening on it.
[02:03] HOLLY: I see. So once the children have changed and gone onto the field, I'll need to keep them inside the designated area.
[02:12] TUTOR: Precisely. You should also check places such as the changing rooms for trip hazards. But your top priority is making sure no child wanders off.
[02:24] HOLLY: Right. I'll need enough staff to help me monitor that.
[02:29] TUTOR: And remember to think about the spectators too.
[02:33] HOLLY: Most of them will probably be parents. I wondered whether they could help us run some of the activities.
[02:40] TUTOR: I wouldn't count on it. They'll be much more concerned with recording their children than with volunteering.
[02:47] HOLLY: Then I'll have to stop them getting in the way while they're doing that.
[02:52] TUTOR: That can be difficult, especially when a proud parent wants a photograph, and you're asking them to stand somewhere else.
[03:01] HOLLY: Understood. What should I consider when I draw up the timetable?
[03:07] TUTOR: Sporting events can be delayed by all kinds of things, including rain. Though fortunately the weather hasn't caused trouble for us so far.
[03:18] HOLLY: I was also thinking about injuries. Someone was hurt last year. Wasn't that what held everything up for such a long time?
[03:26] TUTOR: Yes. And you need a plan for situations like that.
[03:31] HOLLY: Suppose a match finishes level. Should I let the teams continue until one of them wins?
[03:38] TUTOR: That decision will be yours. But whatever you choose, you must allow for it in advance.
[03:47] HOLLY: Right.
[03:50] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the tutorial, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
[04:38] TUTOR: The purpose of the placement is to help you build the skills required in events management. Let's look at those skills now.
[04:48] HOLLY: I think I'm already quite a good communicator. I'm comfortable speaking to people on the phone, booking venues and doing similar tasks.
[04:57] TUTOR: Good. But communication isn't only about your words. Imagine meeting somebody in person and trying to convince them to sponsor an event, for instance.
[05:10] HOLLY: Then I'll need to choose what I wear carefully, of course.
[05:15] TUTOR: Good. Now let's consider organization. Events management is centered on people, so arrangements won't always unfold exactly as planned.
[05:26] HOLLY: So the key is being able to change course when circumstances shift.
[05:31] TUTOR: Exactly. An unexpected problem might force you to alter the timetable immediately.
[05:39] HOLLY: And I should just make the change there and then. Got it.
[05:45] TUTOR: How are you getting on with managing your time?
[05:48] HOLLY: I'm improving. I definitely work better when there's a firm deadline, which is one reason this kind of work suits me.
[05:57] TUTOR: Yes. Although what matters is how you behave when that deadline is getting close.
[06:03] HOLLY: I know. Even if I'm anxious, I have to appear completely composed.
[06:09] TUTOR: Keep reminding yourself that other people mustn't see that you're under pressure.
[06:15] HOLLY: Even when I'm trying to handle several jobs at once.
[06:20] TUTOR: Creativity is another essential skill. Clients often arrive with the broad concept, and the events manager has to work out all the practical points needed to turn it into reality.
[06:35] HOLLY: So I should listen closely to the overall idea, then identify everything that's still missing.
[06:42] TUTOR: Exactly. You will also lead a team. They may offer plenty of suggestions, but the final decisions are yours. Whether refreshments should be served indoors or outside, for example.
[06:57] HOLLY: Wouldn't it be better to let everyone decide together?

[07:01] TUTOR: That sounds fair, but responsibility ultimately rests with you. Back the decision you believe is best and be willing to say that an idea is good but unsuitable for this particular event.
[07:16] HOLLY: I understand. And what about networking? Many students find that worrying because we haven't yet got much professional experience to offer.
[07:27] TUTOR: Experience isn't everything. You can still be an engaging person with worthwhile ideas, and each useful contact you impress may benefit you later.
[07:39] HOLLY: That should help when I start applying for a permanent position.
[07:43] TUTOR: Exactly. Look ahead, remember what you want to achieve, and keep those ambitions in view.
[07:52] HOLLY: Absolutely.
[07:57] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three. You now have one minute to check your answers.

passages.title: Bird Migration Theory
content: 📌 Bird Migration Theory
General overview
Most bird species are thought to make seasonal journeys.
Hibernation theory
An early explanation said birds spent winter below water or concealed in [ _____ ].Experiments with captive birds eventually disproved this idea.
Transmutation theory

Aristotle argued that birds became a different species according to the season.In autumn, he noticed redstarts shedding their [ _____ ] and concluded that they became robins.His reasoning seemed plausible because the two birds were alike in [ _____ ].
17th century
Charles Morton spread the theory that birds travelled to the [ _____ ] during winter.
Scientific developments

In 1822, a stork was shot in Germany carrying an African spear in its [ _____ ].Before this, there had been no [ _____ ] that storks flew to Africa.Until ringing began, researchers knew little about migrating birds' [ _____ ] or the routes they took.Some believed big birds transported smaller ones because the latter were thought unable to cross enormous [ _____ ].Ringing relied on the '[ _____ ]' of dead birds.The first [ _____ ] mapping the movements of European birds appeared in 1931.
transcript: [00:01] AUDIO: You will hear a lecturer discussing how ideas about bird migration developed. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Scientists now believe that most of the world's birds migrate in one way or another.

[01:00] AUDIO: For some species, the seasonal journey is fairly short. They might leave low ground where they spend the winter and move up into the mountains for summer. At the other extreme is the Arctic tern, which travels over 25,000 miles each season between the regions around the North and South Poles. For centuries, people have tried to understand these movements by observing birds.

[01:31] AUDIO: Until quite recently, however, the winter destination of many birds remained a mystery. Without modern scientific methods or technology, people proposed explanations that now seem mistaken and sometimes rather strange. One old theory, dating back about 2,000 years, claimed that birds disappeared beneath seas and oceans to hibernate. A related account suggested that they stayed hidden in mud through the winter and emerged when warmer weather brought food back.

[02:08] AUDIO: The belief in hibernating birds survived for a surprisingly long time. It was not finally rejected until the 1940s when experiments with captive birds showed that they have no instinct to hibernate. Aristotle, the ancient Greek philosopher and naturalist, was among the earliest writers to consider why certain species vanished and returned at particular times of year. From his observations of red starts and robins, he developed the theory of transmutation, the idea that one species became another as the seasons changed.

[02:50] AUDIO: In autumn, he noticed red starts shedding their feathers. He therefore concluded that they turned into robins for winter before changing back into red starts in summer. Although that interpretation was wrong, it is easy to see why it appeared reasonable. The two species are similar in shape.

[03:13] AUDIO: It was a mistaken conclusion drawn from accurate observation. An even more unusual proposal came from Charles Morton, an English amateur scientist of the 17th century. In a paper that was taken more seriously than we might expect, he argued that birds traveled to the moon each year and later returned. To him, this seemed the only rational explanation for the complete seasonal disappearance of some species.

[03:47] AUDIO: A major advance in migration research occurred in 1822 when a white stork was shot in Germany. The bird became famous because a long spear was lodged in its neck, yet had not killed it. It was immediately clear that the weapon was not European, and it was later identified as belonging to a Central African tribe. For ornithology, this discovery was decisive.

[04:17] AUDIO: It provided the first evidence that storks spend the winter in sub-Saharan Africa. The specimen, often called the arrow stork, can still be seen in the zoological collection at the University of Rostock in Germany. Over time, people recognized the broad pattern of European birds traveling south in autumn and north in summer. Even so, precise knowledge remained limited until researchers began catching birds and fitting rings to their legs.

[04:53] AUDIO: Before ringing, almost nothing was known about the destinations reached by individual species or the routes they followed. One suggestion was that large birds acted rather like taxis, carrying smaller birds on their backs. Since some small species weigh only a few grams, many people thought they could not possibly cross vast oceans by themselves. Observations of small birds harassing larger ones were taken as support for this belief.

[05:26] AUDIO: Bird ringing was developed by the Danish schoolteacher Hans Christian Cornelius Mortensen, and it opened the way to many discoveries. The method is still widely used and depends on what researchers call recovery. A ringed bird is found dead at the place to which it migrated and can then be identified. Enormous quantities of information were collected in the early 20th century, revealing for the first time where birds actually spent the winter.
[06:00] AUDIO: In 1931, the first atlas showing the migration of common European species was published and more recent explanations of bird migration.

content: 📌 Easy Life Cleaning Services

Every week

Other services
The company can arrange a plumber or an [ _____ ] when required.A specialist cleaning system helps customers whose allergies are triggered by [ _____ ].
Information about the cleaners

Applicants have a background check involving the [ _____ ] before they are employed.They must provide references.They receive two weeks of [ _____ ].Customers email a [ _____ ] after every visit.The company normally assigns one regular cleaner to each customer.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: Part 1. You will hear a client calling a company about domestic cleaning services. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.
[00:52] JACINTA: Good morning, Easy Life Cleaning Services. Shacinta speaking.
[00:57] CLIENT: Hello. I'm trying to find someone to clean my apartment. Do you provide cleaning for private homes?
[01:06] JACINTA: Yes, we do.
[01:07] CLIENT: Great. It's only a one-bedroom flat. Is there a standard package I can book?
[01:13] JACINTA: Certainly. A flat that size normally takes around two hours. We'd clean every surface properly in each room and polish anything that needs it. Have you got carpets in the apartment?
[01:27] CLIENT: No, there aren't any carpets, though the floor definitely needs to be cleaned.
[01:33] JACINTA: That's included, of course, and we'd clean the floor in every room. We'd also give the kitchen and bathroom a complete clean.
[01:42] CLIENT: That sounds fine.
[01:44] JACINTA: There are extra jobs you can add if you'd like. For instance, we could clean the oven each week.
[01:50] CLIENT: I hardly use the oven, actually. Could you do the fridge instead?
[01:56] JACINTA: No problem. Do you want the fridge cleaned weekly?
[01:59] CLIENT: Yes, definitely. And is ironing something else you can provide?
[02:04] JACINTA: Yes, that's available, too.
[02:06] CLIENT: There wouldn't be a lot. Only the shirts I need for work each week.
[02:11] JACINTA: That's fine. We can also clean the microwave, if that would help.
[02:16] CLIENT: No, I wipe the microwave out quite often, so that won't be necessary.
[02:21] JACINTA: We have other extras that people usually request less frequently, perhaps once a month. We could wash the inside of all your windows, for example.
[02:32] CLIENT: Yes, I'd like that. The flat is on the 15th floor, so specialists regularly deal with the outside. But the windows do get dirty on the inside.
[02:43] JACINTA: We could arrange to have the curtains cleaned as well, whenever that is needed.
[02:48] CLIENT: The curtains are fine. The balcony is another matter, though. It's small and I rarely use it, but it could be washed down about once a month.
[03:01] JACINTA: Yes, we can use a pressure washer on the balcony.
[03:06] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

[03:53] JACINTA: We also offer a few options connected with general home maintenance, if you're interested. If there is a water problem and you urgently need a plumber, for example, we can arrange for a reliable one to come straight away. We can do the same if you need an electrician.
[04:14] CLIENT: That's useful to know. I've only recently moved into the area, so I don't have contacts for people like that yet.

[04:23] JACINTA: Another service you might consider is our specialist vacuum system. It captures as much as 99% of the dust in the air, which improves air quality indoors. That can make a real difference for someone who suffers from allergies.
[04:41] CLIENT: I don't have allergies myself, fortunately, but I'll remember that. Could you tell me something about the people you employ as cleaners?

[04:51] JACINTA: Of course. We select our cleaners very carefully. Every applicant must pass a security check carried out with the police so we know there is no criminal background. And we require references too.

[05:07] JACINTA: If someone appears suitable, we provide two weeks of training, followed by a test. We employ only those who pass. After that, we keep a close eye on their work by asking each client to write a review after every visit and email it to us. That allows us to identify and deal with any problem immediately.
[05:34] CLIENT: Alright, that sounds reassuring. Would the same person come each time?
[05:38] JACINTA: We always try to give each customer one regular cleaner, and in most cases we're able to do that.
[05:46] CLIENT: Good, that's what I wanted. In that case, I'd like to go ahead and...
[05:54] NARRATOR: That is the end of part one. You now have one minute to check your answers to part one.

content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Hotels"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: Part 2. You will hear a speaker giving hotel managers advice about retaining staff. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.

[00:52] AUDIO: Since many of you have spent years working in hotels, you will probably know how disruptive it is when employees keep leaving. A hotel depends on reliable, experienced people to keep its daily operations running well, and frequent changes make everyone's job harder. Why, then, do so many workers move on? Jobs such as cleaning are often low-skilled and poorly paid, and managers commonly blame the wages or the long working hours.

[01:27] AUDIO: What they often overlook, however, is that inadequate training is a major reason for staff leaving. What does rapid staff turnover do to a hotel? Recruiting replacements again and again takes a great deal of time, and while vacancies remain, managers may need to take on some of the missing employees' duties themselves. As a result, they cannot devote enough attention to longer-term matters, such as improving the standard of service.

[01:59] AUDIO: Departures can also damage the confidence of those who stay. Seeing colleagues leave may make them consider going elsewhere, too. How can managers improve the situation? To begin with, they need to avoid simple mistakes that make employees feel unfairly treated.

[02:20] AUDIO: When shifts are arranged, no one should receive special treatment. Everybody should be allowed some say in their schedule, while all employees should share the evening and weekend work. Staff who are treated equally are also more willing to help when an additional person is required. Better staff retention can produce other measurable gains.

[02:45] AUDIO: Consider the Dunwich Hotel. After complaints from employees, it paid for more training and improved working conditions. Complaints subsequently decreased, but that was not the only result. The hotel also found that the average guest spent substantially more during a visit.

[03:05] AUDIO: A customer loyalty program was introduced later and is proving successful. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. I will now describe several approaches to lowering staff turnover, using examples from hotels where I have recently delivered training.

[04:09] AUDIO: Feedback at the Sun Club revealed that employees felt their views were ignored by management. They did not feel like partners with the real part in the hotel's success. That has now changed. Junior employees from every level are invited to regular meetings and encouraged to contribute their ideas.

[04:30] AUDIO: Last year, the Portland decided it needed to put more effort into keeping its staff. Its first move was to establish a program for identifying talented employees. Individuals who appear capable of becoming managers are offered training, in the expectation that a clear path forward will persuade them to remain with the company. At Blue Water Hotels, management chose 50 outstanding employees from across its very large chain.

[05:00] AUDIO: Their reward is a fully funded overseas trip each year. Although enjoyment is an important part of the trip, participants also gain useful knowledge. On the latest visit, for instance, they toured a brewery and learned about a new beer that the hotels would soon offer. Pentlo Hotels found that too many junior receptionists were leaving.

[05:25] AUDIO: To show them that hotel work could provide worthwhile long-term prospects, it launched a management development program. Participants received extra responsibilities and opportunities to experience a range of roles around the hotel. Green Planet aimed to present itself as an employer that genuinely supported its workforce. Many employees had children to care for, so the hotel introduced vouchers that contributed towards their childcare expenses.

[05:59] AUDIO: At the Amesbury, Louise Marsh has achieved one of the industry's strongest staff retention records. Since arriving, she has worked hard to build a helpful, collaborative workplace. She treats the workforce as one large family in which every member matters. That is the end of Part 2.
[06:25] AUDIO: You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 2.

passages.title: Sporting Activities
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Sporting Activities"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: Part 3. You will hear two sports science students, Thomas and Jeanne, discussing Thomas' sporting background and experiences. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
[00:55] JEANNE: So how are you finding the course so far, Thomas?
[00:58] THOMAS: Really good, actually.
[00:59] JEANNE: What made you choose sports science? Back at school, were you hoping to become a professional athlete?
[01:07] THOMAS: Yes, that was definitely my ambition. The other students always expected me to do well. They thought I was exceptionally talented.
[01:16] JEANNE: It must have been nice to be seen that way.
[01:19] THOMAS: It was. I honestly believed I could win almost anything. In running events, I was usually the quickest.
[01:27] JEANNE: So, what changed? Did your parents want you to concentrate on academic work instead?
[01:34] THOMAS: No, they supported me. Looking back, though, I probably didn't apply myself as much as I could have.
[01:42] JEANNE: What do you mean?
[01:43] THOMAS: I relied on natural ability and didn't put enough time into practice.
[01:48] JEANNE: What made you realize that?
[01:50] THOMAS: I was chosen for a two-week training program in Kenya.
[01:54] JEANNE: Kenya? That must have been a surprise.

[01:58] THOMAS: A huge one. They had selected young runners from all over the country and we trained beside some outstanding teenage athletes. I felt incredibly fortunate to have the opportunity. But competing with them showed me that I wasn't as good as I'd imagined.
[02:13] JEANNE: That sounds like a serious shock.
[02:16] THOMAS: It was. At first, I simply couldn't accept that it was happening.
[02:22] JEANNE: I'm sorry. That must have been difficult.
[02:25] THOMAS: I've moved on from it. This university course suits me much better because it introduces us to such a wide range of sports-related fields.
[02:35] JEANNE: That's one of the main reasons I chose it, too.
[02:40] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
[03:27] THOMAS: We need some ideas for next week's discussion session on technology and sport.
[03:32] JEANNE: And we're supposed to include examples from several different sports.
[03:37] THOMAS: Right.
[03:39] JEANNE: We could look at how pieces of sporting equipment developed over time.
[03:43] THOMAS: Good idea. Take table tennis bats. Early ones were eventually covered with rubber that had small raised pimples.
[03:51] JEANNE: Weren't the very first bats just made of wood?
[03:54] THOMAS: They were. Then in the 1920s, a factory was turning out long rubber strips for horse harnesses on a large scale.
[04:06] JEANNE: I wouldn't have connected that with table tennis.
[04:09] THOMAS: Someone did and realized the rubber was ideal for covering a bat.
[04:14] JEANNE: What about cricket? Perhaps we could discuss changes to leg pads.

[04:19] THOMAS: I checked that online, but the pads haven't altered much. The first cricket helmet appeared in 1978, though. The Australian batsman wearing it was booed by the crowd because they thought it looked ridiculous.
[04:34] JEANNE: At least it offered protection. Now helmets are standard.
[04:38] THOMAS: That's different from cycling helmets.
[04:41] JEANNE: Yes, professional cyclists use them, but many people riding ordinary bikes still choose not to.
[04:48] THOMAS: The older designs looked rather like an upside-down bowl.
[04:52] JEANNE: There's a photograph here of a woman wearing one. She seems very pleased with it.
[04:58] THOMAS: Even so, riders working hard often ended up with their hair soaked from the heat inside.
[05:05] JEANNE: Modern helmets have openings that let air circulate so the skin can breathe.
[05:11] THOMAS: We could move on to golf balls and clubs. Golf clubs have changed a lot.
[05:16] JEANNE: The early clubs were entirely wooden, and they snapped so readily that players had to get new ones quite often.
[05:23] THOMAS: Clubs aren't made of wood now, are they?
[05:26] JEANNE: No. Newer materials also allow players to hit the ball much farther.
[05:31] THOMAS: Is hockey equipment similar?
[05:33] JEANNE: Not really. Hockey sticks are still made from wood, and in the early days players commonly shaped their own because there were no ready-made ones to buy.
[05:43] THOMAS: So they weren't being produced commercially. What could we say about footballs?
[05:49] JEANNE: The earliest balls were made from animal skin.
[05:53] THOMAS: Later, stitched leather was used, but it absorbed water whenever matches were played in the rain.
[05:59] JEANNE: Which made the ball increasingly heavy.
[06:02] THOMAS: Exactly. And repeatedly heading that weight could damage a player's neck.
[06:08] JEANNE: That sounds painful.
[06:10] THOMAS: Yes. Well, I think we can put together some useful ideas.
[06:15] NARRATOR: That is the end of Part 3. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 3.

transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: Part 4 You will hear part of a lecture about maple syrup. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Today we're examining another food that comes directly from nature, maple syrup.

[00:56] AUDIO: It may resemble clear honey, but bees play no part in making it. Instead, it comes from the sap that circulates inside maple trees. The finished product is a thick, golden liquid with a sweet flavor. It is sold in bottles or jars, poured over foods such as waffles and ice cream, and used when baking cakes and pastries.

[01:21] AUDIO: Because it contains neither preservatives nor extra ingredients, it is viewed as a healthy substitute for refined sugar. There are numerous kinds of maple tree. They can grow without fertilizer where the soil holds enough moisture, provided they also receive full or partial sunlight during the day and experience very cool nights. Only a few regions offer this combination.

[01:49] AUDIO: They include every part of Canada and the northeastern states of the USA, where the climate is ideal for the trees. Canada supplies more than two-thirds of the world's maple syrup. This helps explain why the five-pointed maple leaf became a national symbol and has appeared on the country's flag since 1964. Maple sugar was being produced by indigenous communities long before Europeans arrived.

[02:19] AUDIO: They made openings in maple trunks and caught the flowing sap in containers formed from tree bark. Since there was no way to store the liquid for long, they heated pieces of rock in the sun until they were extremely hot and placed them in the sap. The liquid was boiled down into sugar, which could then be added to food and drink. Although the method has improved over time, its basic principles remain much the same.

[02:49] AUDIO: Let us now consider present-day production. Maple forests are an important resource for many communities in Canada and the northern United States, so the trees must be carefully maintained. A tree cannot be tapped until its trunk has reached a diameter of roughly 25 cm and that may take as long as 40 years. Sap formation also depends on changing temperatures.

[03:17] AUDIO: During a cold night, the tree draws water from the ground and carries it upwards. Warmer daytime conditions then force that water back down. This continuous movement through the tree creates the sap required for syrup. Once a tree is mature, workers drill a small opening in the trunk and fit a tube that leads into a bucket.

[03:41] AUDIO: A healthy tree can receive several taps without being harmed. The collected sap is about 98% water, with sugar and other nutrients making up the remainder. It must be processed immediately in very large pans called evaporators. A fire beneath each pan heats the liquid until it boils.

[04:04] AUDIO: Water escapes and large volumes of steam are released as the syrup becomes increasingly concentrated. At the right thickness, it is taken off the heat. Workers then filter out a substance known as sugar sand, which would otherwise leave the syrup cloudy and give it a slightly gritty taste. After filtering, the syrup can be packaged for use in many products.
[04:32] AUDIO: The quantities are considerable. Forty litres of sap are needed to produce just one litre of maple syrup. That is the process in outline. In areas such as Quebec where...
[04:47] AUDIO: That is the end of Part 4. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 4.
